text:
Welcome to CLUE!

CLUE is a platform that helps your class figure things out together as a community of scientists and engineers. On clue you can work individually and in a group, and you can share your ideas with the class and see other people's ideas.

In CLUE, everyone works in a group. When you start an activity, you can choose a group. You can change groups by clicking on the group number in the upper right corner. Then, you can either join an existing group or start a new group.

Right now, make sure you are in the same group as the other students you are sitting and working with. You can check what group you're in or change your group in the top right corner.

If your groupmates need help, help them! You're figuring things out together.

tiles.title: Lesson Structure in the Lessons and Resources Pane

text:
Each lesson in CLUE has four parts. The orange tabs above show each part.

You're engineering a new device, and the parts can help you organize your thinking.

  • : That's where you are now! This is where you'll start thinking about a new problem and figuring out the science behind it.

The other three are:

  • Design
  • Develop
  • Evaluate

You'll learn more about these when you get there.

When you're done with one part, go to the next one.

tiles.title: How to pick up a CLUE tile

objects.text: When you hover your mouse over any tile in CLUE, a little triangle will appear that will let you click on the tile and move it to your work space.

text:
Okay, you know the basics! Let's jump into figuring things out!

Biological hands can do a LOT of things! Plus, your brain and muscles are already "wired" to work well with a hand.

Even though we might not make something that looks or works exactly the same, understanding how hands work can give us good ideas about how to design prostheses.

With your partner, find three different ways you can to move an object.

For each way you find, write down what motion or motions are you making with your hand?

When you drag the blue question tile over, you'll be able to write here.

If you want, you can also add a table, take a picture of what you draw, or sketch something.

Record your tile with one of these tile types below. You can also delete tiles if you don't want them anymore, or move tiles around.

objects.text: You can see all the other tile types you can add in the toolbar in the left of your workspace, over there!
Make a table!
Take a pic and post it!
Make a new sketch, or sketch over pictures that you paste!

text:
If you feel like this is too much text on the computer, the section about how hands work is also available in a handout, as well as on the slides.

You may want to go over this as a class. Depending on the level of the class, this may also be a good place to recall prior information or to develop a more complex worksheet.

You probably found a bunch of ways that you can move an object, but how do hands even work?

Researchers from the University of Southern California and MIT used images from MRI, a kind of medical scan, to make simulations of the inside of a hand.

Notice that the fingers have no muscles. When you curl your fingers in, it's actually because your tendons are being pulled.

text:
Go back to where you wrote down the motions you make and draw or write what tendons, muscles, or other parts of your hand you think you use to make that motion.

As you are doing that, also answer the question below (if your screen is still enlarged, will have to bring your workspace back. Here's how you do that)
What is one motion you made that can't be explained by the tendons and muscles you just learned about?

tiles.title: What can you figure out based on that?

text:
What clues or ideas does that give you about what other tendons or muscles there must be in the hand and arm?

If you want an example, look at Dr. Tariq's idea below.

Remember, just like with Dr. Tariq's idea, you can take pictures and upload them, and add labels arrows using the sketch tool!

This is Dr. Tariq. He's a chemist, not a medical doctor, and he doesn't know much about biology.

We were worried this might be confusing, so we showed it to him. Here is the idea he came up with:

objects.text: This is a cartoon, but Dr. Tariq is a real scientist, and this really happened. Here are his real hands making a shadow dog (and he actually likes making shadow puppets!)
"Wooow... that's so interesting! Hmm... what about this?"
"The muscles and tendons you showed explain the motion of my index finger that curls inward"
"There must be some kind of muscle that pulls the fingers out and in, maybe around here. Maybe that's what those muscles in the hand are for..."
"But what about my pinky that goes side to side?"
"Neat! If I press right there [where the blue arrow is] when I move my pinky that way, I can feel the muscle flexing!"
